headline: Man granted first-of-its-kind religious exemption against mandatory AI use at work
summary: A humanist at the University of Kentucky successfully argued that outsourcing his thinking to LLMs like ChatGPT violates his deeply held beliefs, securing a Title VII accommodation.
details: David Durman, a research administrator at the University of Kentucky, has been granted a Title VII religious accommodation. He successfully argued that using AI tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot violates his beliefs as a humanist.

Durman believes that offloading his thinking to AI undercuts his ability to develop as a moral person. He views the process of thinking through work, ethics, and interactions as a key component of his self-development.

The exemption was granted under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination based on religion. Federal courts have previously ruled that humanism qualifies as a religion under this act.

The American Humanist Association (AHA) supported Durman, noting this is the first such accommodation for humanism. AHA staff attorney Alexandria Huiskens stated that humanism, as a comprehensive way of life, deserves the same workplace protections as other religions.

While Title VII exemptions require deep moral conviction and must not impose undue hardship on the employer, Durman is not entirely free from AI. He is still expected to cooperate with colleagues using AI and submit materials to AI tools when necessary.

The widespread adoption of AI in corporate settings has raised many questions, with proponents citing productivity gains. However, reports indicate that many companies outside Big Tech are not yet seeing significant financial returns or clear ROI from AI.

Despite uncertainties, about half of all U.S. employees now use AI in some capacity at work. Durman hopes his story will empower others who feel similarly about mandatory AI use and contribute to a broader discussion on AI's impact.

headline_marked: [[AI disproves 27-year-old Exponential Time Hypothesis]], rendering decades of research 'irrelevant'
headline: AI disproves 27-year-old Exponential Time Hypothesis, rendering decades of research 'irrelevant'
summary: OpenAI and Anthropic have independently shown the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) to be false, a foundational premise in theoretical computer science, impacting vast amounts of existing research.
details: OpenAI and Anthropic have independently claimed to have disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). This 27-year-old hypothesis is a cornerstone of theoretical computer science, and its disproof renders significant bodies of research "dead" or "irrelevant."

ETH posits that the effort to solve certain computational problems increases exponentially with their size. This premise has underpinned vast swathes of research in complexity theory and algorithm design for decades.

The news has sent shockwaves through the academic community. Professor Peter Jonsson expects his upcoming conference presentation to be largely obsolete, while UC Santa Barbara's Daniel Lokshtanov estimates 50 of his papers could become "pointless."

Both AI firms published their proofs on GitHub in natural language and machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has called upon leading computer scientists, including the original proposers of ETH, to verify and unpack these complex AI-generated results.

While the immediate impact is a sense of "doom and gloom" for some researchers, others express excitement. Thore Husfeldt, who formulated a version of ETH, sees it as "fantastic," illuminating an entire subfield for new exploration.

This event highlights AI's accelerating role in scientific advancement, rapidly disproving long-held hypotheses. It raises questions about the future of human-led research in fields where machines can now outperform them.

The rapid influx of AI-generated content, including hundreds of manuscripts from OpenAI, also presents challenges. Researchers are overwhelmed by the volume, with some documents containing errors, making it difficult to digest and verify findings.
